2025.clinched: Race 2, Circuito de Jerez, 19 October 2025, the final race of the season
2025.note: Razgatlıoğlu needed three points at Jerez and started tenth. He was sixth inside two laps and third by lap nine, taking the podium that settled it while Nicolò Bulega won the race and finished 13 points behind, 616 to 603. He could have wrapped it up in the Superpole Race the day before, but Bulega pushed him wide on the opening lap in one of only two retirements he had all year. Thirteen consecutive wins, from Emilia-Romagna in May to Aragón in September, matched the record he had set himself the previous season. It was his third title and his last in the class, before leaving for the premier grand prix class.

2024.clinched: Race 1, Circuito de Jerez, 2024, with two races still to run
2024.note: Razgatlıoğlu needed a top-three finish in the opening race at Jerez and took second behind Nicolò Bulega, ending the year 527 points to 484. It was BMW's first riders' title since the marque entered world superbikes in 2011, and it made him the third rider to win the championship with two different manufacturers. His thirteen straight wins, from Assen to the second race at Portimão, beat the eleven shared by Álvaro Bautista and Jonathan Rea, and the streak ended not on track but in free practice at Magny-Cours, where a crash left him with a mild pneumothorax and cost him two rounds. He returned with the lead down to 13 points and rebuilt it, finishing on the podium in 27 of 30 races.

2023.clinched: Race 1, Circuito de Jerez, 2023, with two races still to run
2023.note: Bautista needed two points, a fourteenth place, and won the race instead: his 26th victory of a season that ended with a record 27, and a lead of 65 points with 37 still available. He became Ducati's first repeat champion since Troy Bayliss in 2006 and the first of its riders to defend the title since Carl Fogarty in 1999, with the riders', teams' and manufacturers' championships all going the same way. Jonathan Rea won once all year, at Most, and finished a distant third in what proved his last season with Kawasaki.

2022.clinched: Race 2, Pertamina Mandalika Circuit, 13 November 2022, one round to spare
2022.note: Bautista went into the race knowing a podium would do it, and finished second behind Razgatlıoğlu, who won all three races in Indonesia. That left 66 points between them with 62 available at the Phillip Island finale. It was his first superbike title, a week before his 38th birthday and sixteen years after his 125cc championship, and Ducati's first since Carlos Checa in 2011. Fourteen wins and 29 podiums from 33 races, in the third season running that a different rider on a different manufacturer took the title.

2021.clinched: Race 1, Pertamina Mandalika Circuit, 21 November 2021, one race to spare
2021.note: Razgatlıoğlu arrived at the final round 30 points clear and finished second to Jonathan Rea in a race delayed by rain and cut to 20 laps, making the pass that mattered on Scott Redding at Turn 1 with three laps left. Rea won, closing the gap to 25, and it changed nothing: Razgatlıoğlu had won more feature races, so the second race could not take the title off him. He was the first Turkish rider to win the championship and the first to beat Rea to it since 2015, ending six consecutive titles. It was Yamaha’s first since 2009, and as in 2009 the marque took the superbike and premier grand prix crowns in the same year.

2020.clinched: Race 1, Autódromo do Estoril, 2020, at the final round
2020.note: Rea needed three points from any of the weekend’s three races. A crash in Superpole had left him fifteenth on the grid, but Scott Redding, starting last after a crash of his own, retired with a technical failure and made the rest academic; Rea came through to fourth while Razgatlıoğlu won from his first pole. He finished on 360 points, 55 clear, and became the first rider to win six consecutive superbike world championships. He had missed his first chance at Magny-Cours, arriving 51 points ahead and winning two of the three races but not the one that would have settled it.

2019.clinched: Race 2, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 2019, with two rounds to spare
2019.note: Rea came to the race 100 points clear needing a win and a non-score from Álvaro Bautista, and got both: on the second lap Razgatlıoğlu lost the rear at the exit of Turn 13 and Bautista could not avoid him. Rea learned of it from a pit board reading BAUTISTA OUT, then held off Michael van der Mark for the win. Bautista, a rookie to the class, had won the first eleven races of the year, a record start, with Rea second in ten of them, before six non-scores in nine races undid him. Laguna Seca was the turn: two wins and a second against three Bautista retirements swung 57 points inside a day. Rea finished on 663 points with 17 wins.

2018.clinched: Race 1, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 2018, with five races to spare
2018.note: Rea had to outscore Chaz Davies by nine points and won the race instead, his thirteenth victory of the year, after passing his pole-sitting teammate Tom Sykes at Turn 3 on the second lap. He became the first rider to win four consecutive superbike titles, drawing level with Carl Fogarty's four, and finished 130 points clear. New performance-balancing rules had been expected to slow Kawasaki down; he won 62% of the races and stood on the podium in 86% of them. He completed the double at Magny-Cours the next day, making it eight wins in a row.

2017.clinched: Race 1, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 30 September 2017, with five races to spare
2017.note: Rea took pole in a wet Superpole despite falling in it, then led from the start and won by 16.3 seconds from Marco Melandri. It was his 50th win in the class, his twelfth of the season, and it made him the first rider to win three successive superbike titles, with an unassailable 129-point lead. His closest rival was his own teammate Tom Sykes. A day later he retired from the second race, caught up in another rider’s crash with his footpeg torn off and his foot injured. He finished the year with 16 wins.

2016.clinched: Race 1, Losail International Circuit, 2016, at the final round
2016.note: Rea needed two points under the floodlights in Qatar, 48 clear of Tom Sykes with 50 available, and became the first rider to defend the superbike title since Carl Fogarty in 1999. He finished on 498 points to Sykes's 447 and Chaz Davies's 445, with nine wins and 23 podiums, and became Kawasaki's first two-time champion. It was less of a procession than the margin suggests: Sykes's Donington double cut the lead to 56, and Davies took back-to-back doubles at Magny-Cours, Jerez and Losail as Ducati found late-season pace.

2015.clinched: Race 1, Circuito de Jerez, 2015, with two rounds to spare
2015.note: Rea needed a single top-ten finish and took fourth, turning a six-point requirement into a 137-point lead with 125 still available. It was his first championship and his first season with Kawasaki, and he ended the year with 14 wins from 26 races and 23 podiums, more wins than any Kawasaki rider had managed in a season. He was the third to take the title on the marque, after Scott Russell in 1993 and his teammate Tom Sykes in 2013, and the first Northern Irishman to win a motorcycle world championship since Joey Dunlop and Brian Reid in 1986. He could have sealed it a round earlier in Malaysia had Chaz Davies not denied him a win late on.

2014.clinched: Race 2, Losail International Circuit, 2014, the final race of the season
2014.note: Guintoli went into the last race three points behind Tom Sykes and won it, taking the championship 416 points to 410. It was the first double victory of his career, and it came in the series’ first night races: he set a lap record passing Jonathan Rea for the lead while Sykes could finish only third. Sykes had led by 44 points after Laguna Seca before Guintoli closed with eight consecutive podiums, arriving in Qatar 12 behind. He was the second French champion in the class, after Raymond Roche in 1990.

2013.clinched: Race 1, Circuito de Jerez, 2013, at the final round
2013.note: Sykes came to the finale 37 points clear of Eugene Laverty, so third place was enough, and third is what he took while Laverty won by passing Marco Melandri around the outside of the last corner. He finished 28 points ahead, with nine wins, eight poles, 18 podiums and 13 fastest laps. He was the first Kawasaki rider to win the championship since Scott Russell in 1993, ending a twenty-year wait and beginning a run of seven titles in eight seasons for the marque, and the fourth British champion after Carl Fogarty, Neil Hodgson and James Toseland. A year earlier he had lost the title by half a point.

2012.clinched: Race 2, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 7 October 2012, the final race of the season
2012.note: Biaggi won the closest championship in the history of the class, 358 points to Tom Sykes's 357.5. He arrived at the final round 30.5 clear, crashed out of the first race in the wet, and started the last one needing fifth place while Sykes needed to win. Sykes won, leading all but the opening lap; Biaggi made a slow start and two early mistakes, then took the position he needed from Davide Giugliano and held it. The half point traced back to shortened races: at Monza the first was cancelled over tyre safety and the second cut to eight laps, which Sykes won for half the score. Biaggi's five victories were the fewest by a champion in a decade, and Sykes led 204 race laps to his 69.

2011.clinched: Race 1, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 2 October 2011, one round to spare
2011.note: Checa needed a thirteenth place and won the race instead, his thirteenth victory of the season, then won the second one as well. He was 107 points clear of Marco Melandri with only Portimão to come. Ducati had closed its factory team, so the title went to the satellite Althea squad in its first year with the marque, having switched from Honda over the winter. He was the first Spaniard to win the championship, and the season brought 14 wins including five doubles, six poles and 20 podiums, with only four races all year in which he finished off the podium.

2010.clinched: Race 2, Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, Imola, 2010, one round to spare
2010.note: Biaggi was eleventh in the first race at Imola after being held up at the start, then abandoned caution in the second and ran at the front. Leon Haslam, the only rider still able to catch him, retired, and Biaggi’s fifth place made it 413 points to 350 with only Magny-Cours left. He was the first Italian to win the superbike championship and the first to win it for Aprilia, in the RSV4’s second season, at 39 and thirteen years after the last of his four consecutive 250cc titles. Aprilia completed the pair eight days later by taking the manufacturers’ championship in France.

2009.clinched: Race 2, Autódromo Internacional do Algarve, 2009, the final race of the season
2009.note: Spies arrived at Portimão 10 points behind Noriyuki Haga, took his eleventh pole of the year while Haga qualified tenth, then won the first race as Haga crashed on the wrong tyre choice. That left him needing fifth in the last race, and fifth is where he finished, with the factory Ducatis of Haga and Michel Fabrizio going one-two ahead of him. He took the title 462 points to 456 with 14 wins in his first season in the class, and became Yamaha’s first superbike champion in a year the marque also won the premier grand prix and supersport championships. He left for the grand prix paddock immediately afterwards.

2008.clinched: Race 1, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 2008, with three races to spare
2008.note: Bayliss took third place in the opening race in France to settle his third title, then won the second for his 50th victory in the class. He had come within three corners of doing it a round earlier at Vallelunga before crashing at a slow corner, which kept Troy Corser and Noriyuki Haga mathematically alive. He finished the year with 410 points, nine wins and sixteen podiums, and signed off at Portimão with a double, taking pole and leading all but one lap of the day before retiring from the sport. His three championships came on three different Ducatis.

2007.clinched: Race 2, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 7 October 2007, the final race of the season
2007.note: Toseland won by two points, 415 to Noriyuki Haga’s 413, and did it from sixth place in the last race while Haga led it from lights to flag. Fog had delayed the day, and a first-corner collision with Lorenzo Lanzi in the opening race dropped Toseland to last before he recovered to seventh, leaving him 17 points ahead going into the decider. He took eight wins on the Honda, one more than anybody else that year, and 14 podiums from 25 races. It was his second title, at the circuit where he had won his first in 2004, and he left for the grand prix paddock after it.

2006.clinched: Race 1, Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, Imola, 4 October 2006, at the penultimate round
2006.note: Bayliss needed fourth place if Noriyuki Haga won, and Haga did not win. Fifth was enough, and once he knew it Bayliss eased off at the Variante Bassa to wave Haga past into fourth. He had arrived at the last two rounds 87 points clear. He won the second race outright, in the rainbow leathers of a world champion, for his first victory at Imola, and the season gave him 12 wins from 24 races including eight in a row, five poles and ten fastest laps. Weeks later he stood in for the injured Sete Gibernau at Valencia and won a grand prix at his only attempt.

2005.clinched: Imola, 2 October 2005, at the penultimate round, after the second race was cancelled
2005.note: Corser’s second title arrived in the strangest way on offer: torrential rain washed the second race out before it started, freezing the standings at 409 points to Chris Vermeulen’s 354 with only 50 still available in France. Vermeulen, the one man who could still have caught him, had won the first race with Corser 0.297 seconds behind. It was Suzuki’s first manufacturers’ championship in the class and its best season since the series began, on the GSX-R1000 in the year factory support returned. Only Vermeulen and Corser’s rookie teammate Yukio Kagayama, who won the opening round in Qatar, stopped him sweeping the first eight races.

2004.clinched: Race 2, Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, 3 October 2004, the final race of the season
2004.note: Toseland went into the closing weekend four points behind his factory Ducati teammate Régis Laconi, won the first race while Laconi finished third, then took second behind Noriyuki Haga in the last one to win the championship 336 points to 327. Laconi had seven wins to Toseland’s three, but five retirements to Toseland’s three, and consistency decided it. At 23, four days short of his birthday, Toseland was the youngest champion the class had had. He had taken the seat vacated by the reigning champion Neil Hodgson, making it two British titles in succession.

2003.clinched: Race 1, TT Circuit Assen, 2003, well before the end of the season
2003.note: Hodgson needed ten points and finished second behind his teammate Rubén Xaus, who took his fourth win of the year; Hodgson then won the second race, ending a run of seven without one. He led 431 points to 291 at that moment. It was a season of near-total Ducati dominance, the 999 taking 20 of the 24 races and no other manufacturer winning at all, after Honda and Aprilia scaled their efforts back. Hodgson won eleven of the first twelve races, missed the podium only four times all year, and became the second British champion in the class after Carl Fogarty.

2002.clinched: Race 2, Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, Imola, 29 September 2002, the final race of the season
2002.note: Edwards arrived one point ahead of Troy Bayliss and left champion by eleven, 552 points to 541, having won both races in front of 97,000 people, the largest crowd for a motorcycle race in Italy. Bayliss took the lead on the last lap of the second race before a mistake at the penultimate corner let Edwards back through. Bayliss had won 14 of the first 17 races and led by 58 points after the first race at Laguna Seca; Edwards then won all nine that remained. Bayliss finished the year with more victories, 14 to 11, and his second places gave Ducati the manufacturers’ title. Edwards never won another world championship race in any class.

2001.clinched: TT Circuit Assen, 2001, at the penultimate round, with a double
2001.note: Bayliss won both races at Assen to settle his first title three weeks before the Imola finale, 51 points clear. The second was decided by team orders: Rubén Xaus led from the thirteenth of sixteen laps, then saw a pit board telling him a Bayliss win with Colin Edwards back in tenth would clinch it, and stuck out a foot on the last lap to wave his teammate through. Edwards, the defending champion, had chosen the wrong front tyre. Bayliss finished 36 points ahead of him and never crashed out of a race all year; a clutch failure at Oschersleben was his only retirement. He was the first rider other than Carl Fogarty to win both races at Assen.

2000.season: thirteen rounds in 2000, and a title settled partly away from the track
2000.note: Edwards took a double at Oschersleben, the penultimate round, to lead by 52 points, but the championship was not safe until the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Noriyuki Haga days before the finale. Haga had tested positive for ephedrine, traced to a herbal supplement, at the opening round in South Africa, and carried a three-week ban and a 45-point deduction. Had the appeal restored those points, Edwards would have led by five with two races left; instead Haga was barred from Brands Hatch and Edwards was confirmed champion. He won eight races on the Honda, which took the title at its first attempt with the VTR1000 SP-1, and finished on 400 points counting only his best eleven results.

1999.season: thirteen rounds in 1999, from Kyalami in March to Sugo in October
1999.note: Fogarty’s fourth and final title was his most emphatic: 489 points to 361, with Colin Edwards and his own teammate Troy Corser level on that score and Edwards taking second place. He won eleven races on the Ducati 996, among them a double at Kyalami where he had broken the lap record in qualifying, another at Monza, and his last home victory at Donington in front of 70,000 people. Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship. He finished his career with four world titles and 59 race wins.

1998.clinched: Sugo, Japan, 1998, at the final round
1998.note: Six points covered the top three arriving in Japan, the closest the championship had been since its first season: Troy Corser led on 328.5, half a point ahead of Aaron Slight, with Fogarty 5.5 further back. Corser could not ride, injured. Slight managed only seventh and sixth. Both races went to the Japanese specialists Akira Ryō and Keiichi Kitagawa, as Sugo races often did, and Fogarty took his third title with only three race wins all year, a remarkably low tally for a champion. He had trailed by 33 points after the eighth round; the arrival of Davide Tardozzi as his team manager turned the season around.

1997.clinched: Race 2, Sugo, Japan, 5 October 1997, at the penultimate round
1997.note: Kocinski finished second in the second race at Sugo to settle the title with a round still to run, then announced he was returning to 500cc grand prix racing. He won nine races on the Honda RC45, which took its only riders’ championship in four seasons of trying and was the last 750cc machine to win the class. It was Honda’s third superbike title after Fred Merkel’s two on the RC30, and Kocinski became the first rider to hold both a superbike world championship and a traditional grand prix one, having won the 250cc title in 1990. His rivalry with Carl Fogarty, who finished second, was genuinely ill-tempered; Fogarty’s season fell apart in a run of crashes as Kocinski found form.

1996.season: twelve rounds in 1996, from Misano in April to Phillip Island in October
1996.note: Corser won seven races to take his first title, and it stayed open late: with three rounds left Aaron Slight still led, Corser 13 points behind, John Kocinski 29 back and Carl Fogarty 45, with 150 points still available. At 24 he was the youngest champion the class had had. He rode for Promotor Racing, the Power Horse Ducati team run by Davide Tardozzi, having finished second for the same squad the year before, and Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship.

1995.season: twelve rounds in 1995, from Hockenheim in May to Phillip Island in October
1995.note: Fogarty’s second title came with thirteen wins, a record for a season at the time, and with two rounds to spare: 478 points to Troy Corser’s 339, with Aaron Slight third on 323. Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship on 580 points to Honda’s 365 and Kawasaki’s 345. The season was overshadowed by the death of Yasutomo Nagai from injuries sustained at Assen, the tenth round; he was fifth in the standings at the time and stayed fifth to the end of the year.

1994.season: eleven rounds in 1994, from Donington in May to Phillip Island in October
1994.note: Fogarty’s first title came by 25 points, 305 to the defending champion Scott Russell’s 280, with Aaron Slight a further three back on 277. He won ten of the 22 races and led the standings from the fourth round to the end, and Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship on 403 points. It was the first of four titles he would win across six seasons.

1993.season: thirteen rounds in 1993, from Brands Hatch in April to Portugal in October
1993.note: Russell won five races and the championship by 29 points, 378.5 to Carl Fogarty’s 349.5, with his own teammate Aaron Slight third on 316. It was Kawasaki’s first riders’ title in the class, and no rider would win another for the marque until Tom Sykes twenty years later. Ducati still took the manufacturers’ championship, on 470 points. A fourteenth round was scheduled and never completed, and the half points in the totals come from races cut short.

1992.season: thirteen rounds in 1992, from Albacete in April to Manfeild in October
1992.note: Polen’s second title was nothing like his first: nine wins rather than seventeen, and a margin of 35 points rather than 150. He finished on 371 to Raymond Roche’s 336, with Rob Phillis third on 288, and Roche was runner-up to him for the second year running. Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship on 502 points.

1991.season: thirteen rounds in 1991, and seventeen wins
1991.note: Polen’s first title remains the benchmark for a dominant season in the class: seventeen race victories out of twenty-six, and 432 points to Raymond Roche’s 282, with Rob Phillis third on 267. Ducati took the manufacturers’ championship on 489. The third round, at Mosport in Canada, was boycotted by the regular riders on safety grounds and run by local entrants instead, with Tom Kipp taking pole and Pascal Picotte the win.

1990.season: thirteen rounds in 1990, from Jerez in March to Manfeild in November
1990.note: Roche was the first French rider to win the championship, and no other did until Sylvain Guintoli in 2014. He took the riders’ title on a Ducati in a season where Honda won the manufacturers’ championship, and he would finish runner-up in each of the next two years, both times to Doug Polen. The calendar ran from March in Spain to November in New Zealand.

1989.season: eleven rounds in 1989, decided by seven points
1989.note: Merkel defended his title on the Honda with three race wins and 272 points, seven ahead of his fellow Honda rider Stéphane Mertens on 265, with Raymond Roche third on 222. Honda took the manufacturers’ championship on 368. Both of his championships were won the same way, on consistency rather than victories: three wins each year, and a margin in single figures each time.

1988.season: the first Superbike World Championship season, in 1988
1988.note: Nine rounds, from Donington Park on 3 April to Manfeild in New Zealand on 3 October, and a finish nearly as close as any that followed: Merkel took it on 99 points from Fabrizio Pirovano’s 93.5 and Davide Tardozzi’s 91.5. Honda won the manufacturers’ championship on 142, with Bimota second on 132.5. The opening round at Donington was scored in a way never repeated, its two race results combined to give a single overall winner. Tardozzi, third that year, went on to manage the teams that won the riders’ title in 1996 and 1998.
